assumptions.summary: Water and electricity demand for each of the five modeled states is treated as constant during one allocation run; this enables equality constraints but suppresses daily, seasonal, price, and emergency response.

Effective water and electricity transport rates on each reservoir-to-state arc are treated as fixed; the linear program therefore excludes congestion, nonlinear loss, outages, and endogenous network adaptation.
Lake Powell and Lake Mead are approximated as cylinders, so volume is converted to head by V/S rather than observed elevation-storage curves.
Only Lake Powell receives external upstream inflow in the printed storage chain; precipitation, tributaries, evaporation, seepage, return flows, and operational releases are not closed.
Direct water and hydropower discharge are represented as separate allocation decisions, while the exact downstream reuse of Powell releases is inconsistent between Equation 4 and Algorithm 1.
Hydropower generation is disabled below a minimum water level and otherwise bounded by a head-proportional capacity relation.
The five included states stand in for the modeled claimant system; Mexico and Gulf/environmental obligations are not included through a complete entity rule.
Each state's resource interest can be summarized by six agricultural, industrial, and residential water/electricity components.
State welfare follows diminishing marginal utility in aggregated water and electricity, with state-specific exponents selected from demand but not published.
States act as rational independent-private-value bidders whose values and distributions support a first-price auction equilibrium.
Auction revenue and fines can finance compensation and renewable-energy investment, and those investments feed back into lower resource pressure.
The control and 50, 70, and 100 percent auction scenarios are treated as comparable policy states despite missing bid and payment details.
Population, agricultural area, industrial area, and renewable-technology share can be perturbed independently to represent more complex conditions.
Repeated waste can be deterred by a progressive monetary penalty augmented by a utility-derived opportunity-cost term.

contributions.summary: A single framework orders physical allocation, economic valuation, auction redesign, sensitivity, conservation, discussion, and public communication.
The RAN represents direct water and hydropower delivery from two serial reservoirs to five claimant states in one directed network.
Separate conservation equations make water and electricity demand explicit rather than burying both resources in one undifferentiated score.
Coupled Powell-Mead state transitions expose the downstream storage handoff and make reservoir depletion time-dependent.
Head-dependent hydropower conversion and minimum-level cutoff connect physical storage to electricity feasibility.
The paper assembles conservation, storage, conversion, capacity, and nonnegativity into a repeated linear optimization problem.
Algorithm 1 turns the static LP into a time-varying planning loop with state updates and a stopping condition.
Trajectories, allocation summaries, and Sankey diagrams expose both temporal depletion and distribution among states.
The six-component resource-interest function distinguishes agricultural, industrial, and residential uses of both water and electricity.
Interest, marginal utility, and value functions create a named interface from physical resources to economic bidding.
The IPV feedback diagram links auctions, fines, compensation, renewable investment, and future resource relief.
The source attempts an asymmetric first-price equilibrium rather than assuming a symmetric closed-form bid.
Generalized backwards shooting and Taylor expansions provide a numerical route for implicit inverse bid functions.
Four scenario rows make allocation and state value changes comparable across increasing auction shares.
Sensitivity examines population, sector area, and renewable technology, connecting the model to demographic and policy change.
The conservation proposal reuses earlier utility concepts in a repeated-offense policy mechanism.
The appended article translates the model chain into nontechnical drought, allocation, feedback, and conservation language.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: The reservoir-decline motivation uses a 2000-2021 Lake Mead elevation graphic, but the artifact does not treat the plotted series as a machine-readable model input.
The task reconstruction comes from the paper's restatement and framework, not from a verbatim official Problem B statement.
Table 1 defines time, flow, demand, transport, storage, level, inflow, area, efficiency, and capacity symbols, but many units and values are absent.
A Colorado River map and two allocation-network diagrams identify the two dams, five states, water arcs, electricity arcs, and downstream direction.
Initial reservoir storage and water levels enter the time-varying state transition; source dates and volume-elevation conversions are not frozen.
Water-demand inputs require a five-state-by-time ledger and alpha transport matrix; neither is published in machine-readable form.
Electricity-demand inputs require a five-state-by-time ledger and gamma transport matrix; neither is published in machine-readable form.
The external Lake Powell inflow v_f and time step Delta t enter the storage update without a published series, unit, or scenario rule.
Hydropower conversion requires density, gravity, dam-specific beta, head, eta capacity, and minimum-level values; only the formula structure is retained.
Table 2 provides minimum and maximum operating levels for Glen Canyon and Hoover dams and seeds the three initial-level scenarios.
Three water-level scenarios condition the RAN run; the exact numeric starting state and daily coefficients must be frozen for replay.
Six sector-level water/electricity interest quantities are proposed for each state, but sources, units, aggregation, and normalization are omitted.
The ratio x_i and aggregate resources y_i and z_i drive valuation; their construction and five state values are not tabulated.
The auction solver requires five value distributions, supports, reserve price, boundary values, and transformed inverse bid states, none of which is published as an input bundle.
Algorithms 2-3 require Taylor coefficients, expansion points, recursion, grid size, and B-spline/root-finding settings; the pseudocode does not provide a replayable configuration.
Table 3 preserves the control and three auction-percentage allocations and value rates, including its visibly incorrect water-level caption.
Sensitivity charts are treated as paper outputs; the perturbation scale, sample grid, recomputation ledger, and raw plotted values are missing.
Ten references provide context for drought, marginal utility, auction theory, backwards shooting, interpolation, and agency data; paper-created transformations remain distinct from cited sources.

models.summary: Separate sufficient-resource allocation, state valuation, scarcity auction, sensitivity, conservation, and public communication into linked deliverables.
Freeze the six stated premises and the time-indexed symbol ledger used by the allocation chain.
Represent two serial reservoirs, five claimant states, direct water, hydropower discharge, electricity delivery, upstream inflow, and Gulf outflow.
Meet each state's effective water demand with direct releases from the two reservoirs.
Meet each state's effective electricity demand from hydropower generated at the two reservoirs.
Update Lake Powell and Lake Mead storage and convert volume to water level under cylindrical geometry.
Convert hydropower discharge and reservoir head to electricity while switching generation off below a minimum level.
Minimize total direct and hydropower discharge while satisfying water, power, storage, head, capacity, and nonnegativity constraints.
Repeatedly select a reservoir-level case, solve the relevant LP, update both reservoirs, and advance the planning horizon.
Compare three initial water-level cases and report storage, allocation, Gulf flow, generation cutoff, and a 21-day replanning result.
Represent state resource interests through agricultural, industrial, and residential water and electricity components.
Map a paper-defined water-electricity ratio to an interest index intended to vary between zero and one.
Convert aggregated water and electricity resources into a state-specific utility using two exponents.
Multiply the interest index by marginal utility to produce each state's private-value input for the auction.
Auction scarce resources, use revenue for compensation and renewable investment, and feed claimed relief back into resource availability.
Define each bidder's first-price bid and printed first-order condition from private value and rivals' transformed distributions.
Express bidder i's expected profit under generalized backwards shooting.
Approximate transformed inverse bid functions and density ratios with Taylor series and iterate Algorithms 2-3.
Compare control, 50, 70, and 100 percent auction scenarios using allocated water and value-growth rates for five states.
Perturb population, agricultural area, industrial area, and renewable-technology share and inspect allocation response.
Increase penalties for repeated waste by combining a base fine with the paper's utility-based opportunity-cost term.
Summarize contributions, weaknesses, future work, conclusions, and the public-facing explanation without treating repetition as new validation.

results_trace.summary: Three initial-level cases are defined from Glen Canyon and Hoover minimum/maximum constraints before the time-varying run.
The paper reports that the sufficient-resource allocation network can meet modeled water and electricity demands for 21 days without additional water.
Generation becomes infeasible before all direct water allocation because reservoir head reaches a plant cutoff.
State-level water and hydropower allocations are summarized in overview charts and then carried into Sankey diagrams.
Water-use and hydropower-use Sankey diagrams preserve source-to-state allocation directions for the RAN result.
The authors recommend rerunning the model every 21 days, conditional on refreshed resources and demands.
Each state receives a resource value defined as its interest index multiplied by marginal utility; the five numeric values are not published.
The control water allocations are 57.0149, 227.3120, 77.6765, 36.3715, and 106.7070 in the table's source units.
The 50-percent auction row repeats the control allocation exactly while reporting nonunit value-growth rates, creating an unresolved intermediate-calculation gap.
The 70-percent auction allocations are 55.0809, 223.3868, 76.8827, 37.1827, and 112.0978 in the table's source units.
The 100-percent auction allocations are 51.0264, 222.0100, 74.5972, 37.3735, and 119.9878 in the table's source units.
The paper interprets increasing auction share as improving total resource value and approaching a Pareto optimum, but supplies no independent welfare certificate.
Population, agricultural-area, and industrial-area perturbations produce plotted duration responses and a claim that adjustment can finish within about three days.
The renewable-technology response is plotted as nearly flat over much of the range before a terminal change; no raw values or scale audit is supplied.
Equation 21 proposes a total fine equal to repeated base fines plus a utility term characterized as opportunity cost.
The Discussion claims flexibility, economic grounding, broad algorithmic applicability, and sustainable feedback while admitting data and assumption limits.
The Conclusion repeats the 21-day RAN horizon, utility-to-value handoff, auction improvement, sensitivity, and conservation policy.
The public article restates auction revenue, compensation, renewable investment, positive feedback, and conservation as the main policy message.

weaknesses.summary: Equation 4 adds only Lake Powell hydropower discharge u_1j to Lake Mead, while Algorithm 1 line 17 visibly adds both v_1j and u_1j; the source does not reconcile the two state transitions.
Equation 9 visibly constrains v_ij and w_ij to be nonnegative but does not constrain the optimized discharge u_ij, suggesting a source-level variable substitution or missing bound.
The time-varying linear program lacks a frozen demand, transport-rate, inflow, area, efficiency, capacity, unit, and initial-state bundle, so the 21-day result is not independently replayable.

The while condition requires both dam levels to remain above their generation minima, yet inner branches discuss depleted-volume cases; stopping, infeasibility, equality, and demand-shortfall behavior are not fully specified.

As printed, Equation 11 simplifies algebraically to 1 wherever defined because 2 ln(e^((x_i+1)/2))/(x_i+1)=1; it therefore cannot express the claimed variation over [0,1] without a missing or misprinted operation.

Equation 12 is singular at mu=1, and the paper selects water and electricity exponents from demand without publishing the values, calibration rule, units, or sensitivity needed to reproduce state valuations.

Equation 15 visibly mixes bidder i and rival j inside the product and uses nested inverse/distribution notation that is not reconciled with Equation 14; the source transcription is retained rather than silently corrected.

Equation 18 visibly prints (t t_0)^j rather than (t-t_0)^j, while Equations 16-20 and Algorithms 2-3 omit boundary values, coefficient recursions, grid size, convergence, numerical tolerances, and executable code.

The IPV result lacks the five valuation distributions, reserve price, bids, fines, Taylor coefficients, initial conditions, solver trace, and equilibrium verification required to reproduce the reported scenario values.
The auction allocation table is visibly captioned 'List of Water Level Constraints', although its rows contain auction ratios, allotted water, and value growth rates.

The 50-percent auction allocation row is identical to the control row while its listed value-rate row is not 1; the paper does not provide the intermediate valuation calculation needed to reconcile allocations, rates, and the Pareto-improvement claim.

The allocation network models five states and later mentions Mexico mainly as compensation, but the paper does not publish a complete basin-entity inclusion rule, demand ledger, Gulf-flow accounting, or consistent state-label audit.

The perturbation charts provide no sampling design, parameter scale, recomputation ledger, uncertainty, interactions, or decision-rank stability; the technology curve is nearly flat before a terminal step.
Equation 21 adds a monetary fine to an unmonetized utility value and calls that utility an opportunity cost without a conversion rate, unit reconciliation, legal basis, or behavioral validation.

The paper reports internal plots and scenario comparisons but no external allocation benchmark, out-of-sample validation, dual or optimality certificate, equilibrium check, uncertainty propagation, or independent operational outcome for its optimal, fair, robust, and sustainable claims.

The two-page article restates the paper's models and conclusions for a public audience but does not add independent evidence; its claims must inherit the main paper's data, formula, solver, validation, and scope boundaries.

writing_logic.summary: The Summary introduces the drought need, names RAN, marginal utility, and IPV, supplies the 21-day headline, then postpones formula and validation detail to the body.

The Introduction moves from reservoir decline to a typed problem restatement and a single framework diagram, so the reader sees physical allocation, economic valuation, scarcity auction, sensitivity, and communication before notation.
Assumptions and notation establish a shared boundary before the RAN, although the paper leaves several units and numerical inputs unstated.
The RAN chapter follows topology -> conservation -> storage -> head -> hydropower -> capacity -> objective and constraints -> Algorithm 1 -> scenarios and plots.
The marginal-utility chapter converts six sector/resource interests into an index, utility, and value, creating an explicit physical-to-economic handoff.
The IPV chapter moves from policy feedback to first-price equilibrium, expected profit, generalized backwards shooting, scenario comparison, and a Pareto-style interpretation.
Sensitivity treats affected-area drivers and renewable technology before the conservation formula, while Discussion separates strengths, weaknesses, and future work.
Conclusion and the appended article repeat the main chain for technical and public audiences; neither repetition is treated as independent validation.
